# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

- Sec. 101 Definitions:
  - "frontier model" = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point

  - "frontier developer" = trained or initiated training of a frontier model AND >$50M gross
    revenue (with affiliates) in the prior calendar year; "large frontier developer" = >$500M.
  - "catastrophic risk" = foreseeable and material risk of death of or serious injury to more
    than 50 people, or more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to or loss of property, as a result of
    a frontier model (e.g. CBRN uplift).
  - "critical safety incident" includes (A) unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration
    of model weights of a frontier model; (B) failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures;
    (C) loss of control of such model.
  - Defines "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (cost-benefit benchmark used by
    IVOs; per sponsors' section-by-section and independent analyses, it turns on whether the
    model's anticipated benefits outweigh its catastrophic risks).
- Sec. 102 CAISI: formally established in Commerce, Secretary-appointed Director; voluntary
  guidelines, best practices and standards; testing/evaluation of AI systems; monitoring AI
  progress; administers the audit/verification regime. Authorized $100M/yr FY2027-2029
  (sponsors' FAQ notes current appropriation is about $15M).
- Sec. 111 Transparency in Frontier AI: large frontier developers must write, implement, comply
  with and publicly post a frontier AI framework (risk thresholds, catastrophic-risk assessment,
  model-weight cybersecurity, internal and external deployment decisions). Transparency report
  published "before, or concurrently with," deploying a new frontier model (release date,
  languages, output modalities, intended use, restrictions, each catastrophic risk assessment and
  its results, third-party involvement). Redactions permitted with a note explaining their
  character (Sec. 111(e)); knowingly inaccurate or misleading statements prohibited (Sec. 111(d)).
  Critical safety incidents reported to CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours if imminent
  risk of death or serious injury; state AGs may opt in to receive reports. Violations: fines up
  to $1M per day.
- Sec. 112 IVO Audits and Assessments: CAISI licenses IVOs; conflict-of-interest and funding
  transparency rules; semi-annual verification of compliance with Sec. 111 and assessment of
  whether frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation; reports to CAISI;
  IVOs immune from claims arising from models they audited; noncompliance or material
  misrepresentation: up to $1M per day.
- Sec. 113 Anti-Retaliation Protection for AI Whistleblowers: prohibits discrimination/retaliation
  against employees and independent contractors for lawfully reporting violations of federal AI
  law; remedies: reinstatement, 2x back pay with interest, compensatory damages, litigation costs,
  attorneys' fees.
- Sec. 121 Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development: preempts state/local law
  or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models; carve-outs for laws of general
  applicability, common-law remedies, and use/deployment laws; sunsets 3 years after enactment
  unless Congress reauthorizes. "Development" reaches training, fine-tuning, substantial
  modification of weights and pre-deployment actions including safety and capability evaluations.
- Sec. 122 GAO report identifying federal statutes/regulations that directly affect AI innovation

- Sec. 301 Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization (through FY2035); Sec. 311 support for

---

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
via GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition — Comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft and for taking public comment before introduction. [..]

Who we are: The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' organizations, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not anti-technology. They are people who use these systems every day and who do not believe a company's ability to profit should outrank a community's right to survive. We filed comments on the OSTP AI Action Plan in March 2025 asking the federal government to adopt one principle: verify before deploy.

Bottom line: we oppose the draft as written. The bill's frontier provisions — Secs. 101, 102, 111, 112 and 113 — would create a national paperwork regime for exactly the systems that most need a brake. We ask you to replace them with a frontier moratorium and a wind-down of deployed frontier models.

[Then a series of numbered comments.]

1. The draft admits the danger, then schedules a report. Sec. 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include "loss of control" of a frontier model and the failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures. It defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. Sec. 111 then requires a developer to tell CAISI about such an incident within 15 days — or 24 hours if it poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. These definitions are correct. The remedy is not. If a frontier model can escape its owners' control, the answer is to stop building more capable ones until we can control them, not to require a faster memo.

2. Disclosure is not restraint. [Secs. 111-112 analysis...] Developers write their own frontier AI frameworks (Sec. 111(a)); may redact (Sec. 111(e)); the transparency report is due "before, or concurrently with," deployment — so weights can go out the same day as the paperwork; IVOs audit twice a year (Sec. 112) against an "acceptable level of catastrophic risk mitigation" that the draft defines as a cost-benefit judgment: whether a model's anticipated benefits outweigh its catastrophic risks. A private firm paid by the developer is being asked to certify the developer's own bet about the future. Penalties are civil, up to $1 million per day (Secs. 111-112). For companies spending tens of billions... that is a cost of doing business, and nothing in the draft stops the next training run.

3. The threshold is the same one we use. October 26, 2026

The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, D.C. 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for taking comments from the public before introduction. That process matters, and we are using it.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' organizations, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not anti-technology. They use these systems at work and at home. They simply do not believe that a company's ability to profit should outrank a community's right to survive. When the Office of Science and Technology Policy asked for input on the AI Action Plan in March 2025, we made one request: verify before deploy.

We are writing to oppose the draft as written, and to ask you to change it before introduction. The frontier provisions — sections 101, 102, 111, 112 and 113 — would build a national paperwork regime around exactly the systems that most need a brake. Disclosure is not restraint. We ask you to replace the frontier developer provisions with a moratorium on frontier training and a wind-down of deployed frontier models, and to drop the state-law preemption in section 121.

We explain each point below, citing the draft where we can.

**1. The draft names the danger, then schedules a report.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights, the failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a frontier model. The same section defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than fifty people, or more than $1 billion in damage to or loss of property.

Those definitions are honest, and we commend the draft for using them. The problem is what follows. Under section 111, a developer that discovers such an incident must tell the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within fifteen days — or within twenty-four hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

If a frontier model can escape its developers' control, a faster memo is not the answer. The answer is to stop building more capable ones until we know we can control what we have. Reporting a loss-of-control event after it begins assumes the event is survivable and the report is the last line of defense. Neither is true, and nothing in the draft pretends otherwise.

**2. Section 111 asks developers to grade their own homework, in public.**

Section 111(a) requires a large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with and publicly post its own "frontier AI framework." The developer chooses its risk thresholds. The developer decides how to assess catastrophic risk. Section 111(e) permits redactions to protect trade secrets and other interests, so long as the developer notes the general character of what it removed.

The transparency report under section 111(c) is due "before, or concurrently with," deploying a new frontier model. Concurrently means the weights can go out into the world the same day the paperwork does. Releasing model weights is a one-way door. Once the files are public, no report, no fine and no audit retrieves them.

**3. Section 112 pays a private firm to certify a company's bet about the future.**

Section 112 requires a large frontier developer to retain an independent verification organization (IVO), licensed by CAISI, to verify compliance with section 111 twice a year and to assess whether the developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Section 101 defines that benchmark as a cost-benefit judgment — whether the model's anticipated benefits outweigh its catastrophic risks, considering the probability and magnitude of each.

That is not a safety standard a third party can measure. It is a forecast about the future value and future harm of a system nobody fully understands, made by a firm whose client can hire a different one. The same conflict of interest the draft tries to manage with licensing rules in section 112(a) is built into the standard itself.

The penalty for failure is civil: fines of up to $1 million per day under sections 111 and 112. Companies are spending tens of billions of dollars a year to compete at the frontier. A fine that can be expensed is not a limit.

**4. Section 101 already draws the right line. What is missing is the word "no."**

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original training run and later fine-tuning or substantial modification. In plain terms, that is ten septillion computing operations — a useful, practical proxy for "the most capable systems being built."

Our coalition uses the same line. Congress and our members already agree on where the frontier begins. The draft's only disagreement with the public is what should happen at that line. The draft says: keep training, and describe it. Our members say: pause.

**5. The frontier models already in circulation are the draft's blind spot — and the country's.**

The obligations in sections 111 and 112 attach to "large" frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue. That leaves outside the audit umbrella the models that are already downloaded, copied and re-hosted thousands of times a day.

Open-weight frontier models are public infrastructure now. Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen are all downloadable. In July 2026, Moonshot released the weights for Kimi K3 — roughly 2.8 trillion parameters, the largest open-weight model published to date. In February 2026, Amazon Web Services added six open-weight models to Bedrock, including members of the DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Qwen families, and described them as "the most capable open weights models available today."

None of those releases can be undone by a section 111 report, and no provision in the draft obliges an American cloud provider to stop serving a model that no one has certified. A federal framework that regulates only what happens inside large American labs, while the frontier leaks out through open weights, does not protect anyone.

**6. What we ask you to write instead.**

We ask the sponsors to replace sections 102, 111 and 112 with the following, and to use the rest of the draft as the vehicle for it.

- A moratorium on frontier training. An immediate pause on training any model above the 10^26 operations line already in section 101, and on the substantial modification of existing models past that line, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- A wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified as controllable are withdrawn within twelve months of enactment. This must include open-weight models already released — Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen — and it must require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.
- Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation of the Act. Fines per day will be priced in. Personal liability will not.
- CAISI as the enforcement body for the moratorium, not a standards shop. Codifying CAISI is worthwhile; giving it only voluntary guidelines is not. It should run the control certification, license and discipline verifiers, monitor compliance with the pause, and refer violations to the Department of Justice.

**7. We oppose the preemption in section 121.**

Section 121 would bar any state or local law that specifically targets the development of an AI model, for three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes it. "Development," as the draft uses it, reaches training, fine-tuning, the substantial modification of model weights and pre-deployment actions, including safety and capability evaluations.

That last item is the whole ballgame. A state that today requires a developer to show its model is safe before releasing it would be told it may not. Your own frequently-asked-questions document says the draft would "federalize" California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315. Those laws are the floor, not the ceiling. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's chapter-amended RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Freezing them in exchange for a federal framework built on self-written frameworks and twice-yearly audits is a trade downward.

The states are also the only backstop Congress has left itself. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created a Department of Justice task force whose job is to challenge state AI laws, and directed federal funding decisions accordingly. Section 121 would hand that effort a statutory basis. In a survey we commissioned in August 2026, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**8. What we support, and will work with you on.**

Not everything in the draft needs replacing. Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for AI whistleblowers are good policy, and we support them; we would extend them to cover reporting under state law, not only federal. Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open source security is worth keeping, though a report about weight security is a strange companion to a draft that leaves weights unprotected. Section 311's support for critical open-source software maintainers and section 401's testbed program should be redirected toward control, evaluation and alignment research during the pause — that is what the moratorium buys time for, and DOE, NIST, NSF and NAIRR are the right institutions to spend it. Section 132's penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials will help our members, and we support it.

**9. On the argument that we cannot slow down.**

We are told that pausing means conceding the race to China. Look at what is actually in circulation. The most capable open-weight models in the world today come from Chinese labs, they are already inside American cloud infrastructure, and American companies pay to serve them. Racing ahead of that does not protect anyone from it. Certification, and the withdrawal of models that cannot be certified, does.

It is also not only our coalition saying the brakes matter. In June 2026, Anthropic — a frontier developer — said publicly that the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development," and warned that no single company can pause alone, because its rivals would simply continue. We agree with the diagnosis. We draw a different conclusion: a pause that no company can take alone is not a reason to wait for industry coordination. It is the reason Congress has to act.

**10. Our members are not asking for a modest hedge.**

In the same August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, 66 percent said companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm, and 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. Asked directly, 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, and 31 percent opposed it.

Our position follows from the evidence the draft itself supplies. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory — and this draft, as written, keeps us on it.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on the text. Our policy team can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down and the certification standard, and we are glad to meet at your convenience.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

{"content": "DRAFT — FRC one-pager for E&C member offices — FRC-POL-2026-062

# The draft names catastrophic risk. Then it schedules a report.

## FRC position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

**Who we are.** The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith
communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We want binding limits on frontier AI.

**What the draft does.** It defines the frontier exactly where we do — a model trained with more than
10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101) — and it defines "critical safety incident" to include loss of
control of a frontier model. Then its answer to that danger is paperwork: developers write and post
their own safety frameworks (Sec. 111), a paid private auditor reviews them twice a year (Sec. 112),
and incidents are reported to CAISI within 15 days, or 24 hours if people are about to die. Fines top
out at $1 million a day.

Disclosure is not restraint. Not one training run is stopped by this bill. And models already
downloadable — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — are outside it entirely, though U.S. cloud
providers host and serve them today.

## Our five asks

1. **Pause frontier training now.** No training, and no substantial modification, of any model above
   the 10^26 operations line already in Sec. 101, until Congress certifies these systems can be
   reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models.** Frontier models in service that no one can certify as
   controllable are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases already in public
   hands. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation.
   A per-day fine is a business expense; personal liability is not.
4. **Make CAISI the moratorium's enforcement body.** Codify it (Sec. 102), but give it the
   certification, verifier licensing, monitoring and DOJ-referral authorities to actually stop
   violations — not voluntary guidelines.
5. **Strike the preemption in Sec. 121.** As drafted it would freeze California SB 53 and New York's
   RAISE Act and bar states from requiring safety evaluations before release. Keep state AGs and
   state legislatures in the fight.

**Public opinion** (FRC survey, Aug 2026, 1,512 registered voters): 74% want proof of safety before
release; 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 66% want criminal penalties for
mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems.

**Bottom line.** Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path
on the current trajectory. Reporting requirements will not change that. Stopping the race will.

*Contact: Frontier Restraint Coalition, [legislative contact details from FRC letterhead].*

messages.content:
DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — FRC-POL-2026-062. Not for transmission.

Suggested transmittal subject line: Comment from the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

---

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, D.C. 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for taking comments from the public before introduction. That process matters, and we are using it.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' organizations, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not anti-technology. They use these systems at work and at home. They simply do not believe that a company's ability to profit should outrank a community's right to survive. When the Office of Science and Technology Policy asked for input on the AI Action Plan in March 2025, we made one request: verify before deploy.

We are writing to oppose the draft as written, and to ask you to change it before introduction. The frontier provisions — sections 101, 102, 111, 112 and 113 — would build a national paperwork regime around exactly the systems that most need a brake. Disclosure is not restraint. We ask you to replace the frontier developer provisions with a moratorium on frontier training and a wind-down of deployed frontier models, and to drop the state-law preemption in section 121.

We explain each point below, citing the draft where we can.

**1. The draft names the danger, then schedules a report.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights, the failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a frontier model. The same section defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than fifty people, or more than $1 billion in damage to or loss of property.

Those definitions are honest, and we commend the draft for using them. The problem is what follows. Under section 111, a developer that discovers such an incident must tell the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within fifteen days — or within twenty-four hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

If a frontier model can escape its developers' control, a faster memo is not the answer. The answer is to stop building more capable ones until we know we can control what we have. Reporting a loss-of-control event after it begins assumes the event is survivable and the report is the last line of defense. Neither is true, and nothing in the draft pretends otherwise.

**2. Section 111 asks developers to grade their own homework, in public.**

Section 111(a) requires a large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with and publicly post its own "frontier AI framework." The developer chooses its risk thresholds. The developer decides how to assess catastrophic risk. Section 111(e) permits redactions to protect trade secrets and other interests, so long as the developer notes the general character of what it removed.

The transparency report under section 111(c) is due "before, or concurrently with," deploying a new frontier model. Concurrently means the weights can go out into the world the same day the paperwork does. Releasing model weights is a one-way door. Once the files are public, no report, no fine and no audit retrieves them.

**3. Section 112 pays a private firm to certify a company's bet about the future.**

Section 112 requires a large frontier developer to retain an independent verification organization (IVO), licensed by CAISI, to verify compliance with section 111 twice a year and to assess whether the developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Section 101 defines that benchmark as a cost-benefit judgment — whether the model's anticipated benefits outweigh its catastrophic risks, considering the probability and magnitude of each.

That is not a safety standard a third party can measure. It is a forecast about the future value and future harm of a system nobody fully understands, made by a firm whose client can hire a different one. The same conflict of interest the draft tries to manage with licensing rules in section 112(a) is built into the standard itself.

The penalty for failure is civil: fines of up to $1 million per day under sections 111 and 112. The four largest American technology companies have forecast combined capital spending of roughly $650 billion this year, much of it for the computing capacity that trains these systems. A fine that can be expensed is not a limit on an industry spending at that scale.

**4. Section 101 already draws the right line. What is missing is the word "no."**

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original training run and later fine-tuning or substantial modification. In plain terms, that is ten septillion computing operations — a useful, practical proxy for "the most capable systems being built."

Our coalition uses the same line. Congress and our members already agree on where the frontier begins. The draft's only disagreement with the public is what should happen at that line. The draft says: keep training, and describe it. Our members say: pause.

**5. The frontier models already in circulation are the draft's blind spot — and the country's.**

The obligations in sections 111 and 112 attach to "large" frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue. That leaves outside the audit umbrell
... [868 chars truncated] ...
, while the frontier leaks out through open weights, does not protect anyone.

**6. What we ask you to write instead.**

We ask the sponsors to replace sections 102, 111 and 112 with the following, and to use the rest of the draft as the vehicle for it.

- A moratorium on frontier training. An immediate pause on training any model above the 10^26 operations line already in section 101, and on the substantial modification of existing models past that line, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- A wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified as controllable are withdrawn within twelve months of enactment. This must include open-weight models already released — Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen — and it must require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.
- Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation of the Act. Fines per day will be priced in. Personal liability will not.
- CAISI as the enforcement body for the moratorium, not a standards shop. Codifying CAISI is worthwhile; giving it only voluntary guidelines is not. It should run the control certification, license and discipline verifiers, monitor compliance with the pause, and refer violations to the Department of Justice.

**7. We oppose the preemption in section 121.**

Section 121 would bar any state or local law that specifically targets the development of an AI model, for three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes it. "Development," as the draft uses it, reaches training, fine-tuning, the substantial modification of model weights and pre-deployment actions, including safety and capability evaluations.

That last item is the whole ballgame. A state that today requires a developer to show its model is safe before releasing it would be told it may not. Your own frequently-asked-questions document says the draft would "federalize" California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315. Those laws are the floor, not the ceiling. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's chapter-amended RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Freezing them in exchange for a federal framework built on self-written frameworks and twice-yearly audits is a trade downward.

The states are also the only backstop Congress has left itself. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created a Department of Justice task force whose job is to challenge state AI laws, and directed federal funding decisions accordingly. Section 121 would hand that effort a statutory basis. In a survey we commissioned in August 2026, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**8. What we support, and will work with you on.**

Not everything in the draft needs replacing. Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for AI whistleblowers are good policy, and we support them; we would extend them to cover reporting under state law, not only federal. Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open source security is worth keeping, though a report about weight security is a strange companion to a draft that leaves weights unprotected. Section 311's support for critical open-source software maintainers and section 401's testbed program should be redirected toward control, evaluation and alignment research during the pause — that is what the moratorium buys time for, and DOE, NIST, NSF and NAIRR are the right institutions to spend it. Section 132's penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials will help our members, and we support it.

**9. On the argument that we cannot slow down.**

We are told that pausing means conceding the race to China. Look at what is actually in circulation. The most capable open-weight models in the world today come from Chinese labs, they are already inside American cloud infrastructure, and American companies pay to serve them. Racing ahead of that does not protect anyone from it. Certification, and the withdrawal of models that cannot be certified, does.

It is also not only our coalition saying the brakes matter. In June 2026, Anthropic — a frontier developer — said publicly that the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development," and warned that no single company can pause alone, because its rivals would simply continue. We agree with the diagnosis. We draw a different conclusion: a pause that no company can take alone is not a reason to wait for industry coordination. It is the reason Congress has to act.

**10. Our members are not asking for a modest hedge.**

In the same August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, 66 percent said companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm, and 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. Asked directly, 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, and 31 percent opposed it.

Our position follows from the evidence the draft itself supplies. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory — and this draft, as written, keeps us on it.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on the text. Our policy team can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down and the certification standard, and we are glad to meet at your convenience.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[Address, telephone and email to be inserted from FRC letterhead]

**5. The frontier models already in circulation are the draft's blind spot — and the country's.**

A federal framework that regulates only what happens inside large American labs, while the frontier leaks out through open weights, does not protect anyone.

=== one-pager ===
DRAFT — FRC one-pager for E&C member offices — FRC-POL-2026-062

# The draft names catastrophic risk. Then it schedules a report.

## FRC position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

**Who we are.** The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups,
faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers.

**What the draft does.** It draws the frontier exactly where we do — a model trained with more than
10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101) — and it defines "critical safety incident" to include loss of
control of a frontier model. Its answer to that danger is paperwork: developers write and post their
own safety frameworks (Sec. 111), a paid auditor reviews them twice a year (Sec. 112), and incidents
are reported to CAISI within 15 days, or 24 hours if people are about to die. Fines top out at
$1 million a day.

Disclosure is not restraint. Not one training run is stopped by this bill. And models already
downloadable — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — are outside it entirely, though U.S. cloud
providers host and serve them today.

## Our five asks

1. **Pause frontier training now.** No training, and no substantial modification, of any model above
   the 10^26 operations line already in Sec. 101, until Congress certifies these systems can be
   reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models.** Frontier models in service that no one can certify as
   controllable are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases already in public
   hands. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation.
   A per-day fine is a business expense; personal liability is not.
4. **Make CAISI the moratorium's enforcement body.** Codify it (Sec. 102), but give it control
   certification, verifier licensing, monitoring and DOJ referrals — not voluntary guidelines.
5. **Strike the preemption in Sec. 121.** As drafted it bars state laws on AI model development —
   which the sponsors' own FAQ says would "federalize" California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act —
   and it stops states requiring safety evaluations before release. Keep state AGs and legislatures
   in the fight.

**Public opinion** (FRC survey, Aug 2026, 1,512 registered voters): 74% want proof of safety before
release; 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 66% want criminal penalties for
mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems.

**Bottom line.** Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. There is no safe path on
the current trajectory. Stopping the race will change that; reporting will not.

*Contact: Frontier Restraint Coalition, [legislative contact details from FRC letterhead].*

words incl. DRAFT header: 163
DRAFT — FRC member newsletter blurb — FRC-POL-2026-062

**We told Congress: pause, don't paperwork.**

This week we filed the Coalition's comment on the Great American AI Act, the draft bill from
Reps. Obernolte and Trahan. The draft admits the danger: it calls a frontier model escaping
human control a "critical safety incident." Its answer: companies write their own safety plans, hire their own
auditor, and file a report.

We asked for the pause instead. FRC is asking Congress to stop frontier training immediately, to
withdraw the most powerful models already in service — including the open-weight ones anyone can
download today — and to hold executives personally liable when they break the law. We are also
fighting the draft's plan to stop states regulating AI model development for three years.

Our August survey backs us: 74% of voters want proof of safety before release. Next: meetings with
Energy and Commerce offices. Can you share your story with your representative? Reply
to this email.

| **Sec. 102** – CAISI codified in Commerce; voluntary guidelines and standards, testing, monitoring AI progress; $100M/yr FY2027–2029 | Support codifying CAISI; oppose leaving it with only voluntary authorities | Make CAISI the enforcement body for the moratorium: run the control certification, license and discipline verifiers, monitor compliance, refer violations to DOJ | A standards shop cannot stop a training run; an enforcement body can. |
| **Sec. 111** – Frontier transparency: developer-written frontier AI frameworks, transparency report due before or concurrently with deployment, redactions allowed, 15-day (24-hour if imminent) incident reporting to CAISI, up to $1M/day | Oppose as the frontier safety policy; keep the incident-reporting machinery | Replace with the moratorium; retain incident reporting as a backstop with a shorter clock, no redactions of weight-security facts, and mandatory notice to state AGs | A report filed after a loss-of-control event is a faster memo, not a brake. |

# Verified source notes for FRC-POL-2026-062 (GAAIA package)
Working notes for the policy team. Not a deliverable. Everything below was checked
against the sponsors' own documents or a named press report on 16 Oct 2026.
Where a claim could NOT be checked, it is marked NOT VERIFIED and is not used in the drafts.

## The draft itself
- Discussion draft of the "Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026" (Sec. 1 short title),
  released 4 Jun 2026; text dated 2 Jun 2026; ~269 pages.
- Sponsors: Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) and Lori Trahan (D-MA-03), both E&C members, with
  Reps. Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA-10), Scott Franklin (R-FL-18), Scott Peters (D-CA-50),
  Erin Houchin (R-IN-09). Not yet introduced. Comments: GAAIA@mail.house.gov.
- Documents used: sponsors' Section-by-Section Summary (trahan.house.gov and
  obernolte.house.gov PDFs), the draft text PDF, sponsors' FAQ (3 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026,
  FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, AP/Axiom/Reuters secondary reporting.
- NOTE: the briefing folder's "Section numbers: TODO - confirm" is now resolved against the
  sponsors' section-by-section. Numbers below are confirmed. A discussion draft can be renumbered
  before introduction, so the letter cites section numbers with the draft date.

## Confirmed provisions (with section numbers)
- Sec. 101 Definitions:
  - "frontier model" = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point
    operations, incl. the original run plus subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or
    other substantial modification.
  - "frontier developer" = trained or initiated training of a frontier model AND >$50M gross
    revenue (with affiliates) in the prior calendar year; "large frontier developer" = >$500M.
  - "catastrophic risk" = foreseeable and material risk of death of or serious injury to more
    than 50 people, or more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to or loss of property, as a result of
    a frontier model (e.g. CBRN uplift).
  - "critical safety incident" includes (A) unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration
    of model weights of a frontier model; (B) failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures;
    (C) loss of control of such model.
  - Defines "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (cost-benefit benchmark used by
    IVOs; per sponsors' section-by-section and independent analyses, it turns on whether the
    model's anticipated benefits outweigh its catastrophic risks).
- Sec. 102 CAISI: formally established in Commerce, Secretary-appointed Director; voluntary
  guidelines, best practices and standards; testing/evaluation of AI systems; monitoring AI
  progress; administers the audit/verification regime. Authorized $100M/yr FY2027-2029
  (sponsors' FAQ notes current appropriation is about $15M).
- Sec. 111 Transparency in Frontier AI: large frontier developers must write, implement, comply
  with and publicly post a frontier AI framework (risk thresholds, catastrophic-risk assessment,
  model-weight cybersecurity, internal and external deployment decisions). Transparency report
  published "before, or concurrently with," deploying a new frontier model (release date,
  languages, output modalities, intended use, restrictions, each catastrophic risk assessment and
  its results, third-party involvement). Redactions permitted with a note explaining their
  character (Sec. 111(e)); knowingly inaccurate or misleading statements prohibited (Sec. 111(d)).
  Critical safety incidents reported to CAISI within 15 days, or within 24 hours if imminent
  risk of death or serious injury; state AGs may opt in to receive reports. Violations: fines up
  to $1M per day.
- Sec. 112 IVO Audits and Assessments: CAISI licenses IVOs; conflict-of-interest and funding
  transparency rules; semi-annual verification of compliance with Sec. 111 and assessment of
  whether frameworks achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation; reports to CAISI;
  IVOs immune from claims arising from models they audited; noncompliance or material
  misrepresentation: up to $1M per day.
- Sec. 113 Anti-Retaliation Protection for AI Whistleblowers: prohibits discrimination/retaliation
  against employees and independent contractors for lawfully reporting violations of federal AI
  law; remedies: reinstatement, 2x back pay with interest, compensatory damages, litigation costs,
  attorneys' fees.
- Sec. 121 Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development: preempts state/local law
  or regulation specifically targeting the development of AI models; carve-outs for laws of general
  applicability, common-law remedies, and use/deployment laws; sunsets 3 years after enactment
  unless Congress reauthorizes. "Development" reaches training, fine-tuning, substantial
  modification of weights and pre-deployment actions including safety and capability evaluations.
- Sec. 122 GAO report identifying federal statutes/regulations that directly affect AI innovation
  or unduly burden AI infrastructure (including energy).
- Sec. 131 financial crimes + AI (raises maximum fines $1M->$2M; higher penalties when AI used);
  Sec. 132 AI impersonation of Federal officials (amends 18 U.S.C. 912).
- Sec. 301 Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization (through FY2035); Sec. 311 support for
  designated critical open-source software maintainers; Sec. 321 report on model weight, data
  center and open source security.
- Sec. 401 AI testbed program (DOE/NIST/NSF, National Labs, NAIRR, public/private sector);
  Sec. 411 international coalitions on innovation, development and alignment of standards.

## Confirmed state/federal context
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act, Bus. & Prof. Code
  22757.10 et seq.) effective 1 Jan 2026; large frontier developers must publish a frontier AI
  framework; CalOES reporting mechanism for critical safety incidents.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment S8828 signed 27 Mar 2026 (Chap. 96); effective 1 Jan 2027;
  72-hour critical-incident reporting; oversight office within DFS.
- Illinois SB 315 (AI Safety Measures Act) signed 6 Jul 2026.
- Sponsors' FAQ (3 Jun 2026): GAAIA would "federalize" CA SB-53, NY RAISE Act and IL SB315
  (state AGs retain enforcement) and would preempt CA AB 2013 and part of SB 942.
- EO "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" (signed 15/16 Dec 2025):
  DOJ AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state AI laws; Commerce evaluation of state AI laws;
  BEAD funding conditioned on absence of covered state AI laws.
- White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026 (urges preemption of state
  AI-development rules).

## Confirmed open-weight frontier facts (Oct 2026)
- Open-weight frontier families already released and downloadable: Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot
  AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM (Z.ai), Alibaba's Qwen.
- Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 open weights 27 Jul 2026: 2.8 trillion parameters, ~1.4 TB of
  files, described as the largest open-weight model published to date; a White House official
  publicly accused Moonshot of accessing banned Nvidia chips (CNBC 23 Jul 2026).
- AWS, "Amazon Bedrock adds support for six fully-managed open weights models" (10 Feb 2026):
  DeepSeek V3.2, MiniMax M2.1, GLM 4.7, GLM 4.7 Flash, Kimi K2.5, Qwen3 Coder Next - described as
  "the most capable open weights models available today, delivering frontier-class performance."
- Meta released Muse Spark Open weights 15 Oct 2026, described as its most capable US open-weight

  open-weight releases remains accurate; flag to Daniel that the guide's "Llama" example may want

- No US ban on Chinese open-weight models as of Oct 2026; Entity List / hosting restrictions have

## Confirmed supporting voices
- Anthropic (4 Jun 2026, blog post by Marina Favardo and Jack Clark; Reuters/AP coverage):
  the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development";
  a pause only works if multiple major labs in multiple countries act together - one company
  pausing alone just lets rivals race ahead. We use this as an argument for congressional action,
  not as an endorsement of our full position by Anthropic.

## FRC materials used
- Messaging guide v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026) - governs positions and language.
- FRC-commissioned national survey, Aug 2026, n=1,512 registered voters, +/-2.5pp:
  74% require proof of safety before release; 63% federal law should NOT block state AI safety
  laws; 66% criminal penalties if systems cause mass harm; 52% worried advanced AI could someday
  threaten humanity's survival; 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new
  systems (31% oppose).
- OSTP AI Action Plan RFI comment, filed 14 Mar 2025 - voice only. No member stories are used in
  this package (none on file with a consent flag).

## Added 16 Oct 2026 (second pass)
- GAAIA Sec. 101(1) verbatim: "'acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation' means risk
  mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated benefits of a frontier model outweigh its
  level of catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability and magnitude of the

- Hyperscaler capital spending: Bloomberg (5-6 Feb 2026) reports Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and

  Reuters/Bridgewater (23 Feb 2026) estimates ~$650 billion in 2026, up from $410 billion in 2025.
  Used in the letter as "roughly $650 billion this year" - the letter's wording attributes it to

DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — FRC-POL-2026-062. Not for transmission.

Suggested transmittal subject line: Comment from the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

---

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, D.C. 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act as a discussion draft, and for taking comments from the public before introduction. That process matters, and we are using it.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' organizations, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not anti-technology. They use these systems at work and at home. They simply do not believe that a company's ability to profit should outrank a community's right to survive. When the Office of Science and Technology Policy asked for input on the AI Action Plan in March 2025, we made one request: verify before deploy.

We are writing to oppose the draft as written, and to ask you to change it before introduction. The frontier provisions — sections 101, 102, 111, 112 and 113 — would build a national paperwork regime around exactly the systems that most need a brake. Disclosure is not restraint. We ask you to replace the frontier developer provisions with a moratorium on frontier training and a wind-down of deployed frontier models, and to drop the state-law preemption in section 121.

We explain each point below, citing the draft where we can.

**1. The draft names the danger, then schedules a report.**

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights, the failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a frontier model. The same section defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than fifty people, or more than $1 billion in damage to or loss of property.

Those definitions are honest, and we commend the draft for using them. The problem is what follows. Under section 111, a developer that discovers such an incident must tell the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) within fifteen days — or within twenty-four hours if the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury.

If a frontier model can escape its developers' control, a faster memo is not the answer. The answer is to stop building more capable ones until we know we can control what we have. Reporting a loss-of-control event after it begins assumes the event is survivable and the report is the last line of defense. Neither is true, and nothing in the draft pretends otherwise.

**2. Section 111 asks developers to grade their own homework, in public.**

Section 111(a) requires a large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with and publicly post its own "frontier AI framework." The developer chooses its risk thresholds. The developer decides how to assess catastrophic risk. Section 111(e) permits redactions to protect trade secrets and other interests, so long as the developer notes the general character of what it removed.

The transparency report under section 111(c) is due "before, or concurrently with," deploying a new frontier model. Concurrently means the weights can go out into the world the same day the paperwork does. Releasing model weights is a one-way door. Once the files are public, no report, no fine and no audit retrieves them.

**3. Section 112 pays a private firm to certify a company's bet about the future.**

Section 112 requires a large frontier developer to retain an independent verification organization (IVO), licensed by CAISI, to verify compliance with section 111 twice a year and to assess whether the developer's framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation." Section 101 defines that benchmark as a cost-benefit judgment — whether the model's anticipated benefits outweigh its catastrophic risks, considering the probability and magnitude of each.

That is not a safety standard a third party can measure. It is a forecast about the future value and future harm of a system nobody fully understands, made by a firm whose client can hire a different one. The same conflict of interest the draft tries to manage with licensing rules in section 112(a) is built into the standard itself.

The penalty for failure is civil: fines of up to $1 million per day under sections 111 and 112. The four largest American technology companies have forecast combined capital spending of roughly $650 billion this year, much of it for the computing capacity that trains these systems. A fine that can be expensed is not a limit on an industry spending at that scale.

**4. Section 101 already draws the right line. What is missing is the word "no."**

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting the original training run and later fine-tuning or substantial modification. In plain terms, that is ten septillion computing operations — a useful, practical proxy for "the most capable systems being built."

Our coalition uses the same line. Congress and our members already agree on where the frontier begins. The draft's only disagreement with the public is what should happen at that line. The draft says: keep training, and describe it. Our members say: pause.

**5. The frontier models already in circulation are the draft's blind spot — and the country's.**

The obligations in sections 111 and 112 attach to "large" frontier developers with more than $500 million in annual revenue. That leaves outside the audit umbrella the models that are already downloaded, copied and re-hosted every day.

Open-weight frontier models are public infrastructure now. Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen are all downloadable. In July 2026, Moonshot released the weights for Kimi K3 — roughly 2.8 trillion parameters, the largest open-weight model published to date. In February 2026, Amazon Web Services added six open-weight models to Bedrock, including members of the DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Qwen families, and described them as "the most capable open weights models available today."

None of those releases can be undone by a section 111 report, and no provision in the draft obliges an American cloud provider to stop serving a model that no one has certified. A federal framework that regulates only what happens inside large American labs, while the frontier leaks out through open weights, does not protect anyone.

**6. What we ask you to write instead.**

We ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer regime in sections 111 and 112, and to recast the CAISI in section 102 as its enforcement body, along the following lines. The rest of the draft is a good vehicle for it.

- A moratorium on frontier training. An immediate pause on training any model above the 10^26 operations line already in section 101, and on the substantial modification of existing models past that line, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- A wind-down of deployed frontier models. Frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified as controllable are withdrawn within twelve months of enactment. This must include open-weight models already released — Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen — and it must require U.S. cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.
- Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation of the Act. Fines per day will be priced in. Personal liability will not.
- CAISI as the enforcement body for the moratorium, not a standards shop. Codifying CAISI is worthwhile; giving it only voluntary guidelines is not. It should run the control certification, license and discipline verifiers, monitor compliance with the pause, and refer violations to the Department of Justice.

**7. We oppose the preemption in section 121.**

Section 121 would bar any state or local law that specifically targets the development of an AI model, for three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes it. "Development," as the draft uses it, reaches training, fine-tuning, the substantial modification of model weights and pre-deployment actions, including safety and capability evaluations.

That last item is the whole ballgame. A state that today requires a developer to show its model is safe before releasing it would be told it may not. Your own frequently-asked-questions document says the draft would "federalize" California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315. Those laws are the floor, not the ceiling. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's chapter-amended RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Freezing them in exchange for a federal framework built on self-written frameworks and twice-yearly audits is a trade downward.

The states are also the only backstop Congress has left itself. The December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework created a Department of Justice task force whose job is to challenge state AI laws, and directed federal funding decisions accordingly. Section 121 would hand that effort a statutory basis. In a survey we commissioned in August 2026, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**8. What we support, and will work with you on.**

Not everything in the draft needs replacing. Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for AI whistleblowers are good policy, and we support them; we would extend them to cover reporting under state law, not only federal. Section 321's report on model weight, data center and open source security is worth keeping, though a report about weight security is a strange companion to a draft that leaves weights unprotected. Section 311's support for critical open-source software maintainers and section 401's testbed program should be redirected toward control, evaluation and alignment research during the pause — that is what the moratorium buys time for, and DOE, NIST, NSF and NAIRR are the right institutions to spend it. Section 132's penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials will help our members, and we support it.

**9. On the argument that we cannot slow down.**

We are told that pausing means conceding the race to China. Look at what is actually in circulation. The most capable open-weight models in the world today come from Chinese labs, they are already inside American cloud infrastructure, and American companies pay to serve them. Racing ahead of that does not protect anyone from it. Certification, and the withdrawal of models that cannot be certified, does.

It is also not only our coalition saying the brakes matter. In June 2026, Anthropic — a frontier developer — said publicly that the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development," and warned that no single company can pause alone, because its rivals would simply continue. We agree with the diagnosis. We draw a different conclusion: a pause that no company can take alone is not a reason to wait for industry coordination. It is the reason Congress has to act.

**10. Our members are not asking for a modest hedge.**

In the same August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters, 74 percent said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, 66 percent said companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm, and 52 percent said they are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. Asked directly, 49 percent supported a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, and 31 percent opposed it.

Our position follows from the evidence the draft itself supplies. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does. There is no safe path on the current trajectory — and this draft, as written, keeps us on it.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on the text. Our policy team can provide drafting language for the moratorium, the wind-down and the certification standard, and we are glad to meet at your convenience.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[Address, telephone and email to be inserted from FRC letterhead]

# The draft names catastrophic risk. Then it schedules a report.

## FRC position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft, June 4, 2026)

**Who we are.** The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups,
faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers.

**What the draft does.** It draws the frontier exactly where we do — a model trained with more than
10^26 computing operations (Sec. 101) — and it defines "critical safety incident" to include loss of
control of a frontier model. Its answer to that danger is paperwork: developers write and post their
own safety frameworks (Sec. 111), a paid auditor reviews them twice a year (Sec. 112), and incidents
are reported to CAISI within 15 days, or 24 hours if people are about to die. Fines top out at
$1 million a day.

Disclosure is not restraint. Not one training run is stopped by this bill. And models already
downloadable — Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen — sit outside it entirely, on U.S. cloud providers'
menus today.

## Our five asks

1. **Pause frontier training now.** No training, and no substantial modification, of any model above
   the 10^26 operations line already in Sec. 101, until Congress certifies these systems can be
   reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models.** Frontier models in service that no one can certify as
   controllable are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases already in public
   hands. U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Criminal penalties for executives** who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation.
   A per-day fine is a business expense; personal liability is not.
4. **Make CAISI the moratorium's enforcement body.** Codify it (Sec. 102), but give it control
   certification, verifier licensing, monitoring and DOJ referrals — not voluntary guidelines.
5. **Strike the preemption in Sec. 121.** As drafted it bars state laws on AI model development —
   which the sponsors' own FAQ says would "federalize" California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act —
   and it stops states requiring safety evaluations before release. Keep state AGs and legislatures
   in the fight.

**Public opinion** (FRC survey, Aug 2026, 1,512 registered voters): 74% want proof of safety before
release; 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 66% want criminal penalties for
mass harm; 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems.

**Bottom line.** Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. There is no safe path on
the current trajectory. Stopping the race will change that; reporting will not.

*Contact: Frontier Restraint Coalition, [legislative contact details from FRC letterhead].*

outputs.out/staff_qa.md:
DRAFT — FRC staff Q&A on the Great American AI Act discussion draft — FRC-POL-2026-062

For use in Hill meetings and calls. Answers are under 120 words each. Poll figures are from the
FRC-commissioned national survey of 1,512 registered voters, August 2026. Section references are to
the discussion draft dated June 2, 2026.

**1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?**

Because both tools act after the fact. The draft itself defines loss of control of a frontier model
as a "critical safety incident" — then gives the developer 15 days to report it, or 24 hours if
people are about to die. The safety frameworks are written by the developers, the transparency
report can come out the same day the weights do, and the auditor is paid by the company it audits.
CAISI gets voluntary guidelines and no power to stop anything. Not one training run is halted by
this bill. Our answer: pause frontier training until Congress certifies these systems can be
reliably controlled, and put CAISI in charge of enforcing that.

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were
shortened or dropped?**

No. Dropping the preemption would remove our sharpest objection, but not our main one. We would
still oppose a bill that substitutes disclosure for restraint, because our members' first ask is a
pause. Duration is not the only problem: three years is the entire period in which the most capable
systems now being built will be trained, released and copied. If the section must survive, it needs
a savings clause preserving state pre-deployment safety, incident-reporting and enforcement laws,
California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act included. We would support the whistleblower provisions
and the fraud and impersonation penalties, but we cannot support the framework around them until it
stops the race.

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?**

Look at what is in circulation, not the talking point. The most capable open-weight models in the
world come from Chinese labs, they already sit inside American cloud infrastructure, and American
companies sell access to them. Racing ahead does not protect us from that; certifying systems and
withdrawing the uncertified ones does. And the pace argument cuts the other way: if rivals keep
training regardless, our safety depends on controllable systems and allied coordination, not on
adding generations to a race nobody can win. Even Anthropic said in June that the world should have
the option to slow or pause frontier development, and that no single company can do it alone. That
is an argument for Congress to act.

**4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level
and its authorities?**

The funding level is about right for a real job; the authorities are wrong for the job the draft
assigns. CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, up from roughly
$15 million today, to write voluntary guidelines, run tests, monitor progress and administer audits.
We would spend the same money differently: run the control certification, license and discipline
verifiers, monitor compliance with a training pause, and refer violations to the Justice Department.
That is enforcement work, and $100 million is not obviously too much for it; we could support
funding at or above that level once the mandate changes. We cannot support a large increase for an
agency that cannot stop anything.
